tagline: A story bible that feeds itself into the prompt while you draft the next scene.
verdictSummary: Novelcrafter's actual trick is small and specific: it keeps a codex of characters, places and lore, notices which entries a scene mentions, and quietly assembles them into the context window before the model drafts. That is a matching pass plus a prompt builder, and it is a weekend at most. What takes longer is the manuscript furniture around it — the scene board, the revision history, the export that produces a manuscript an editor will accept — and that is where the weekend becomes a fortnight.
coreLoopDIY: Keep characters, places and lore as entries in a local codex, write scenes in a chapter tree, and let the drafting prompt automatically include only the codex entries that scene actually references.
whatYouLose: the mature scene board and outlining views built over years of author feedback
prompt presets contributed by a community of working novelists
sync between a desktop and a laptop mid-manuscript
the polish of an editor that never loses a chapter
whyPeopleStillPay: Because at four dollars a month the subscription is cheaper than the evening you would spend rebuilding it, and a manuscript is not the thing you want to be beta-testing your own file format on.
notes: The codex-matching step is the whole idea; a build that only offers a chat sidebar next to a text editor has missed the point of the product entirely.
prompt:
Build a local novel-drafting app whose defining feature is a codex that injects itself into the drafting prompt.

Data model, in SQLite: a project holds chapters, chapters hold scenes, and a scene holds Markdown text. Alongside that, a codex of entries, each with a type (character, place, object, faction, concept), a canonical name, a list of aliases, a body of notes, and a set of relationships to other entries.

The matching pass is the core. When the user asks for a draft or a continuation of a scene, scan the scene's existing text and its one-line summary for codex names and aliases. Build the prompt from: the project's style notes, the summaries of the two preceding scenes, the full text of the current scene, and the notes of every matched codex entry plus its first-degree relations. Show the assembled context to the user before sending, as a collapsible list of what was included and why, and let them add or remove an entry for this call only. Never send the whole codex; the point is selection.

Drafting actions: continue the scene, rewrite the selection with an instruction, and expand a one-line beat into prose. Insert every result as a suggestion the user accepts, rejects or edits — never write directly into the manuscript.

Manuscript views: a chapter tree with drag-to-reorder, a per-scene status (outline, draft, revised, done), a running word count with a daily target, and a scene board showing point-of-view character and summary as cards.

Export: a single Markdown file, a compiled DOCX with chapter breaks, and a full JSON backup of manuscript plus codex.

Use Anthropic or OpenAI, whichever key is configured. With no key, everything except the three drafting actions must still work — the codex, the manuscript and the export are the parts you cannot afford to lose.

Out of scope: cloud sync, collaboration, any hosted service, and shipping bundled prompt presets. The user writes their own.

faq.q: Can I import my Novelcrafter project?
faq.a: Partly. Novelcrafter exports the manuscript as Markdown and the codex as a structured file, so scenes and entries come across. Relationships between codex entries and any saved prompts do not map cleanly and need rebuilding by hand.

faq.q: Which model should I point it at?
faq.a: For prose continuation the larger models are noticeably better at holding voice, and the difference is worth more here than in most tasks. The codex matching means each call sends a few thousand tokens rather than the whole book, so the cost difference between a small and a large model is smaller than you would expect.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Model calls only. A scene continuation with a handful of codex entries attached is a few thousand tokens in and a few hundred out, so cents. Drafting a full novel this way lands in the tens of dollars, which is roughly a year of the Hobbyist plan.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Working on the same manuscript from two machines. Novelcrafter syncs; this stores a SQLite file on one computer. Putting that file in a sync folder mostly works and occasionally corrupts, which is not a risk worth taking with a manuscript.
